claims.claim: Mount Tambora erupted in April 1815 in the largest eruption in recorded history, losing over a kilometre of summit height
claims.definition: the April 1815 eruption of Mount Tambora on Sumbawa, Indonesia, is ranked VEI 7, the largest known historic eruption; the summit elevation was reduced by more than a kilometre (from roughly 4,300 m to about 2,850 m)
claims.current_record_holder: largest known eruption in recorded history (VEI 7)
claims.measured_value: VEI 7; summit height reduced by roughly 1,300-1,400 m
claims.authoritative_source: Oppenheimer, 'Climatic, environmental and human consequences of the largest known historic eruption: Tambora volcano (Indonesia) 1815', Progress in Physical Geography 27 (2003); Self, Gertisser et al. field studies
claims.notes: narration says 'the largest eruption in recorded history' and 'more than a kilometre of its summit' — both defensible

nuance.note: VEI 7 ranking and summit collapse magnitude are standard volcanology

claims.claim: Tambora injected tens of millions of tonnes of sulfur into the stratosphere, where global winds spread a planet-wide veil
claims.definition: the eruption injected an estimated ~50-60 Tg of sulfur dioxide into the stratosphere, oxidizing to sulfate aerosols that circled the hemisphere within months; the stratosphere is above the weather, so the aerosols were not rained out quickly
claims.measured_value: estimates ~40-60 Tg SO2 (tens of millions of tonnes); residence time roughly 1-3 years
claims.authoritative_source: Oppenheimer, Progress in Physical Geography 27 (2003); Sigl et al., 'Timing and climate forcing of volcanic eruptions for the past 2,500 years', Nature 523 (2015)
claims.notes: narration deliberately says 'tens of millions of tonnes' to match the published range; 'above the rain' carries the residence-time point

nuance.note: stratospheric injection and global aerosol spread are well established; the exact total varies by reconstruction (ice-core based)

claims.claim: stratospheric sulfate aerosols scattered sunlight and cooled the planet by roughly half a degree Celsius in 1816
claims.definition: stratospheric sulfate aerosols scatter and absorb solar radiation; reconstructions put the 1816 global mean surface temperature anomaly at roughly -0.4 to -0.7 degrees Celsius relative to surrounding years
claims.measured_value: 1816 global-mean anomaly of about -0.4 to -0.7 degC depending on reconstruction; narration says 'roughly half a degree'
claims.authoritative_source: Sigl et al., Nature 523 (2015); Oppenheimer, Progress in Physical Geography 27 (2003); Raible et al., 'Tambora 1815 as a test case for high impact volcanic eruptions', WIREs Climate Change (2016)
claims.notes: narration hedges with 'roughly half a degree'; the small-number-huge-consequence contrast is the beat's point

nuance.note: the cooling is firmly established; the exact global-mean magnitude varies across reconstructions (0.4-0.7 degC), so narration stays at 'roughly half a degree'

claims.claim: in 1816 June snow fell on New England and killing frosts recurred through the summer months
claims.definition: documented weather records describe June 1816 snow across northern New England and killing frosts in June, July and August 1816, with dates recorded in contemporary diaries and almanacs ('eighteen-hundred-and-froze-to-death')
claims.measured_value: June snowfall in New England 1816 (documented); frosts in each summer month
claims.authoritative_source: Oppenheimer, Progress in Physical Geography 27 (2003); Post, 'The Last Great Subsistence Crisis in the Western World' (1977); contemporary New England weather records
claims.notes: narration avoids specific snowfall amounts; 'every summer month' matches the documented June/July/August frosts

nuance.note: the 1816 New England summer anomalies are among the best-documented weather events of the era

claims.claim: the 1816 harvest failures brought soaring prices, famine and food riots; historians describe it as the last great subsistence crisis of the Western world
claims.definition: the 1816-17 harvest failures across Europe and North America drove grain prices to record highs, sparked food riots, and caused famine conditions in parts of Europe and Asia; historian John D. Post characterized it as the last great subsistence crisis in the Western world
claims.measured_value: qualitative historical characterization; narration attributes the phrase to historians
claims.authoritative_source: Post, 'The Last Great Subsistence Crisis in the Western World' (1977); Oppenheimer, Progress in Physical Geography 27 (2003)
claims.notes: narration says 'historians still call it' — the phrase is Post's, widely repeated in the literature

nuance.note: harvest failure and social consequences are documented; the 'last great subsistence crisis' phrasing is historiographical, hence attributed

claims.claim: the 1816 climate anomaly was traced to the 1815 Tambora eruption only decades later, after the veil had settled
claims.definition: contemporaries did not connect the strange weather of 1816 to Tambora; the volcanic attribution developed through 19th-20th century science (Franklin's 1784 'dry fog' analogy, later aerosol climatology), long after the aerosol veil had settled out
claims.measured_value: qualitative: attribution established long after the event; narration avoids pinning a date
claims.authoritative_source: Oppenheimer, Progress in Physical Geography 27 (2003); Raible et al., WIREs Climate Change (2016)
claims.notes: narration says 'for years, no one connected' and 'only decades later' implicitly via 'traced ... only decades later' in the claim; the payoff stays qualitative

nuance.note: the delayed attribution story is well documented in the history of science
